blocks.md: **Window invariant: while valid, record answer, then shrink from left. Each pointer crosses ≤ n ⇒ O(n) despite nested-looking loops.**
**Window validity rules:** positives-only ⇒ shrink works. Negatives inside ⇒ window logic breaks (monotonicity gone) — that's L3/L4 territory (deque/prefix tricks).

items.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock I
items.statement: One transaction max profit. Single pass tracking min-so-far.

solutionCode.label: track the cheapest price seen so far

items.complexity: Time O(n), single pass. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why must the min update come after the profit check?
followups.a: If you update first, minSoFar can become today’s own price and you would book a zero profit from buying and selling on the same day. The ordering encodes the "buy strictly before sell" rule.

followups.q: Prices only fall, e.g. [7,6,4,3,1]. What is returned?
followups.a: 0. Every `x - minSoFar` is negative and `best` starts at 0, which represents making no transaction at all — exactly what the problem allows.

items.title: Maximum Subarray (Kadane)
items.statement: Classic — trace table above is your proof-of-understanding.
hints: All-negative case handled by same formula.

solutionCode.label: Kadane: extend or restart

followups.q: Why seed with a[0] instead of 0?
followups.a: Seeding with 0 assumes the empty subarray is allowed. On an all-negative array like [-3,-1,-2] that wrongly returns 0; seeding with a[0] returns -1, the best non-empty subarray.

followups.q: How would you return the indices, not just the sum?
followups.a: Track a tentative start that resets whenever `cur` restarts (i.e. when a[i] > cur + a[i]), and commit start/end into saved variables each time `best` improves.

items.title: Majority Element
hints: Counter cancel pairs of distinct values.

solutionCode.label: Boyer-Moore vote, then verify

items.complexity: Time O(n) for two passes. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why does the cancelling argument work?
followups.a: Pair every majority element with a distinct one; each pair cancels to zero. Because the majority appears more than n/2 times, it cannot be fully cancelled, so it is what remains standing at the end.

followups.q: What changes for elements appearing more than n/3 times?
followups.a: You carry two candidates and two counters instead of one — at most two values can exceed n/3. The verification pass becomes mandatory rather than defensive, since either candidate may not actually qualify.

items.title: Product of Array Except Self

solutionCode.label: prefix products forward, suffix running backward

items.complexity: Time O(n) in two sweeps. Space O(1) beyond the output array.

followups.q: Why is division banned, beyond it being an arbitrary rule?
followups.a: Division breaks on zeros — you cannot divide the total product by a zero element. Handling it means special-casing one zero versus two or more, which is more branching than the two-sweep version needs.

followups.q: Is the output array counted as extra space?
followups.a: Conventionally no; the problem explicitly excludes it. Say so — then point out the running `right` scalar is the only genuine extra storage, so it is O(1) by the stated definition.

items.title: Find Pivot Index
items.statement: Left sum == right sum position. Trace above mirrors it.
hints: Total first, then sweep comparing pre[i].

solutionCode.label: total minus left minus self is the right side
solutionCode.py:
def pivot_index(a: list[int]) -> int:
    total, left = sum(a), 0
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        if left == total - left - x:   # right side = total - left - a[i]
            return i
        left += x
    return -1

followups.q: Does index 0 or n-1 qualify as a pivot?
followups.a: Yes. An empty side sums to 0, so index 0 is a pivot when the rest of the array sums to 0. That is the case most naive implementations get wrong by starting the scan at 1.

followups.q: Negative numbers are allowed — does that break anything?
followups.a: No. The identity right = total − left − a[i] is pure arithmetic and never assumes positivity. A prefix-sum approach that relies on monotonic growth would break; this one does not.

items.title: Container With Most Water
items.statement: Max area between lines. Prove pointer-move safety out loud.

solutionCode.label: two pointers, always discard the shorter wall

followups.q: Justify discarding the shorter wall.
followups.a: Area is width × min(h[l], h[r]). Keeping the shorter wall and moving the taller one strictly reduces width while min() cannot rise above the shorter wall — so every such pair is no better than the one just measured. Nothing optimal is lost.

followups.q: How is this different from Trapping Rain Water, which looks similar?
followups.a: Here you pick exactly two lines and ignore everything between them. There, every bar contributes and the interior heights matter. Same two-pointer shape, different invariant.

items.title: Two Sum II (sorted)
items.statement: Indices of pair hitting target — no hashmap allowed this time.
hints: State why each move discards safely.

solutionCode.label: converge from both ends on a sorted array

followups.q: Why is each pointer move safe?
followups.a: If a[l]+a[r] < target, then a[l] paired with anything at or below r is also too small, since a[r] is the largest remaining. So a[l] can be discarded entirely. The mirror argument retires a[r] when the sum is too large.

followups.q: What if the array were not sorted?
followups.a: Two pointers stop working — the discard argument depends on ordering. You would use a hash map from value to index for O(n) time at O(n) space, which is the original Two Sum.

items.title: Maximum Average Subarray I
hints: Running sum slide; divide once at end.

solutionCode.label: fixed window, divide once at the end
solutionCode.py:
def find_max_average(a: list[int], k: int) -> float:
    s = sum(a[:k])
    best = s
    for i in range(k, len(a)):
        s += a[i] - a[i - k]     # one in, one out
        best = max(best, s)
    return best / k

followups.q: Why compare sums rather than averages inside the loop?
followups.a: Every window has the same width k, so dividing by k is a monotonic transform that cannot change which window wins. Deferring the division avoids n floating-point divisions and the rounding noise they bring.

followups.q: Why `long long` for the sum?
followups.a: With n up to 10^5 and values up to 10^4, a window sum can reach 10^9 — close enough to the 32-bit ceiling that a slightly larger constraint would overflow silently.

items.title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
items.statement: Shortest window with sum ≥ target (positives guaranteed).

solutionCode.label: grow right, shrink left while still valid
solutionCode.py:
def min_sub_array_len(target: int, a: list[int]) -> int:
    l, s, best = 0, 0, float('inf')
    for r, x in enumerate(a):
        s += x
        while s >= target:            # shrink while still satisfying
            best = min(best, r - l + 1)
            s -= a[l]
            l += 1
    return 0 if best == float('inf') else best

items.complexity: Time O(n) — each index enters and leaves the window once. Space O(1).

followups.q: The inner loop looks like it makes this O(n²). Why is it O(n)?
followups.a: Amortisation: `l` only ever increases and never passes `r`, so across the whole run the inner loop body executes at most n times total. Each index is added once and removed once.

followups.q: What breaks if negative numbers are allowed?
followups.a: The window stops being monotonic — adding an element can shrink the sum, so "shrink while sum ≥ target" no longer safely retires the left edge. You would need prefix sums with a deque or a sorted structure instead.

items.title: Maximum Sum Circular Subarray
items.statement: Circular wrap allowed. Two Kadanes: max vs (total − min); handle all-negative trap.
hints: If kadaneMax < 0 → whole array negative → return kadaneMax only.

solutionCode.label: best normal window vs total minus worst window
solutionCode.py:
def max_subarray_sum_circular(a: list[int]) -> int:
    total = 0
    cur_max, best = 0, float('-inf')
    cur_min, worst = 0, float('inf')
    for x in a:
        total += x
        cur_max = max(x, cur_max + x); best = max(best, cur_max)
        cur_min = min(x, cur_min + x); worst = min(worst, cur_min)
    # all-negative: the wrapped candidate would be the empty subarray
    return max(best, total - worst) if best > 0 else best

followups.q: Why does a wrapping subarray equal total minus a middle subarray?
followups.a: A wrapped selection is a prefix plus a suffix. Its complement is exactly one contiguous middle block, so maximising the wrap is the same as minimising that middle block. That is why one Kadane runs on minimums.

followups.q: What is the all-negative trap?
followups.a: If every element is negative, the minimum subarray is the whole array, so total − worst = 0 — which corresponds to selecting nothing. The problem requires a non-empty subarray, so you must fall back to the plain Kadane maximum.

revisionCard: pre[r+1]−pre[l] = range sum; long long discipline
Subarray-sum-k with negatives = prefix-count hashmap (seed freq[0]=1)
Two-pointer safety = exchange argument; say WHY moves are safe
Window: expand right, record while valid, shrink left; O(n) amortized
Negatives break windows — escalate to L3/L4 tools
Kadane: cur=max(x,cur+x); circular = max(kadane, total−minKadane) w/ all-negative guard
